passages.t: ‘The fool says in his heart’: Psalm 14 again
passages.happening:
If this psalm sounds familiar, it is. It is almost the same as Psalm 14. “The fool says in his heart, ‘There is no God.’ They are corrupt; their ways are vile. There is no one who does good” (verse 1).

God looks down “to see if any understand, if any seek God” (verse 2). He finds no one. “All have turned away, they have together become corrupt; there is no one who does good, not even one” (verse 3).

The evildoers “devour my people like bread” (verse 4). But verse 5 is new. “For God has scattered the bones of those who besieged you. You put them to shame, for God has despised them” (verse 5).

The end is the same longing as Psalm 14. “Oh, that the salvation of Israel would come from Zion!” (verse 6).
passages.hearers:
Why have the same psalm twice? It seems to have been kept in two collections. The changes are telling. Where Psalm 14 says ‘the LORD’, Psalm 53 says ‘God’ every time. That fits Book Two's habit, explained in the note on Psalm 42. The heading adds “According to Mahalath” (verse 1), a musical word whose meaning is not known.

The largest change is verse 5. Psalm 14 says, “God is in the company of the righteous” (Psalm 14:5). Psalm 53 speaks instead of an army that besieged the city and was scattered. It seems the old psalm was fitted to a new rescue, though no one knows which. Leaving bones unburied was a deep disgrace in the ancient world.

The note on Psalm 14 explains the ‘fool’: not someone slow-witted, but someone who lives as if God does not matter.
passages.later:
Paul quotes these lines to show that all people need God's mercy: “There is no one righteous, not even one. There is no one who understands, no one who seeks God” (Romans 3:10-11). His point is that Jew and Gentile alike stand in the same need.

The cry for ‘salvation from Zion’ is answered, for Christians, in the one who came to Zion. Paul writes later in the same letter, “The Deliverer will come from Zion” (Romans 11:26).
passages.asks:
The Bible repeats itself here on purpose. Some truths need saying twice. The fool's thought, ‘God does not matter’, is not only a skeptic's thought. It is the quiet thought behind much of ordinary life, in church as well as out of it.

The psalm's answer is not an argument. It is a longing: that God's rescue would come. Read the note on Psalm 14 beside this one.

Does ‘no one who does good’ mean nobody ever does a kind thing? No. Plenty of people do. The psalm looks from God's side: is anyone seeking him? The note on Psalm 14 explains why the ‘fool’ is not a word aimed at honest unbelievers, and how Paul turns verse 3 on everyone, religious people included.
